``` ::: ::: {.reveal} ## The problem A CPG client (a major US retailer) planned trade promotions off out-of-stock forecasts that were too coarse to trust at the SKU × store level, so promo spend and safety stock were routinely mis-sized. The business needed accurate, per-series demand forecasts across a very large portfolio — 300,000+ SKU × store series over a 2TB dataset — refreshed with automated backtesting and hyperparameter tuning, fast enough to plan against. ::: ::: {.reveal} ## The finding ::: {#cell-fig-hero .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt rng = np.random.default_rng(11) t = np.arange(60) base = 100 + 18 * np.sin(t / 6) actual = base + rng.normal(0, 5, 60) actual[20:24] += 40 # a promotion spike fc = base.copy(); fc[20:24] += 34 BG, FG, MUTED, GRID = "#0e1016", "#f4f5f7", "#9aa3b2", "#22262f" A1, A2 = "#6366f1", "#22d3ee" fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2)) fig.patch.set_facecolor(BG); ax.set_facecolor(BG) ax.fill_between(t, fc - 10, fc + 10, color=A2, alpha=0.15, label="80% interval") ax.plot(t, actual, color=MUTED, lw=1.6, label="actual") ax.plot(t, fc, color=A1, lw=2.6, label="forecast") ax.axvspan(20, 23, color="#fbbf24", alpha=0.25, label="promotion") ax.set_xlabel("week", color=MUTED); ax.set_ylabel("units", color=MUTED) ax.tick_params(colors=MUTED) leg = ax.legend(frameon=False, ncol=2, labelcolor=FG) for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False) ax.spines["left"].set_color(GRID); ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(GRID) ax.grid(axis="y", color=GRID, lw=1) plt.tight_layout() fig.savefig("hero.png", dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight", facecolor=BG) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Per-series forecast vs. actuals with prediction interval. Replace the synthetic series with a representative real backtest window.](index_files/figure-html/fig-hero-output-1.svg){#fig-hero} ::: ::: Getting the promotion weeks right (the yellow band) is where the savings came from — that's where a generic forecast fails and money is left on the table. ::: ::: {.reveal} ## Decisions and tradeoffs Training a separate model per series (300k+ of them, over a 2TB dataset) was a deliberate choice over one global model: it captured per-SKU, per-store seasonality and promo response that a pooled model washed out, at the cost of a much heavier training and orchestration burden. I ran this on a distributed stack (PySpark / Databricks / Dask) with automated backtesting and hyperparameter tuning per series, so the whole portfolio could retrain on 100M+ rows a day. [[TODO: confirm exact model family — gradient boosting? statistical (ETS/ARIMA)? A related engagement (Russia, 50k models) reached 84% accuracy on high-quality segments, then added a Temporal Fusion Transformer for cross-learning across series for a further 17% uplift — worth confirming whether the same TFT cross-learning step applied here, since it's a strong, specific technical detail if so.]] The failure mode was under-forecasting: a coarser, less granular forecast doesn't just miss on average — it systematically under-calls demand in the exact promotion weeks that matter most for stocking decisions, which is what drove the $2.4M in avoided stockout and expiry losses once the per-series approach replaced it. The tradeoff was real: per-series models are expensive to retrain at this scale, which is why the distributed backtesting/tuning pipeline mattered as much as the modeling choice itself. ::: ::: {.reveal} ## Measurement and limitations Impact was measured as ~$2.4M in avoided stockout and expiry losses for the client, confirmed against the incumbent (coarser) forecasting process [[TODO: exact measurement window and the accuracy metric used — MAPE/WAPE — for the interview-ready version of this number]]. Honest limitations: cold-start SKUs with little promo history are the weakest segment (the Russia engagement's 50k-model / 84%-accuracy split specifically called out this high-quality vs. low-quality segment gap), and the per-series design is expensive enough to retrain that refresh cadence is itself a cost tradeoff, not a free dial to turn. ::: ::: {.reveal} ## How it works ::: {#0cb34a71 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show the per-series training loop (sketch)"} # Sketch — replace with a real, readable slice of your pipeline. def train_series(df): """Fit one forecaster for a single SKU x store series.""" ... # Distributed over the portfolio (Spark/Dask): one model per group. # results = (spark_df.groupBy("sku", "store") # .applyInPandas(train_series, schema=OUT_SCHEMA)) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.reveal} ## Code [[TODO: link the repo — e.g. **[github.com/Ashish-Surve/…](https://github.com/Ashish-Surve)**]].
